newsitem.title: UK: Britain to boost swinging image to lure tourists.
newsitem.headline: Britain to boost swinging image to lure tourists.

text.p: Britain will try to increase already record numbers of foreign tourists next year by boosting its image as the place for young, cultured and active holidaymakers, senior industry officials said on Monday.
Attempting to portray itself as a fashionable country enjoying a major cultural renaissance, Britain welcomed a record three million tourists in August.

"Style is part of life and people should therefore come to the creative cookhouse for what is innovating and exciting," British Tourist Authority (BTA) chief executive Anthony Sell told a news conference.
Last month the U.S. magazine Newsweek declared London to be "the coolest place on earth" and Sell said he wanted to attract "the young and those who still feel young".
The BTA will also be promoting the idea of golf, cycling and walking holidays, the so-called "soft adventure" market.
The English Tourist Board (ETB) will continue its "Style and Design" campaign to highlight British popular music, cuisine, nightlife, architecture, decorative arts and fashion.

Tourists interested in visiting locations where films and television series were shot will be able to find more details on the BTA's so-called Movie Map, which is now accessible on the Internet at http://www.bta.org.uk. David Quarmby, chairman of both the BTA and ETB, said he expected a record 26 million people to visit the country this year and spend a total of 13 billion pounds ($21 billion).
"We are benefiting from the trend away from beach holidays and towards cultural breaks," he said. Last year 23.7 million foreign tourists visited Britain and spent 11.9 billion pounds ($19 billion).

But he said growth rates could be threatened by the problems identified in a report last month by the Department of National Heritage (DNH), which said the industry was being harmed by unskilled staff, low pay and high turnover of employees.
The report said British tourism industry workers were half as productive as their counterparts in the United States and France.

"It's a very fragmented industry and difficult to raise standards...There is a major role for the big hotel and attractions to play. Some are beacons of hope but I think more can be done," Quarmby said in an interview.
Last year a DNH study showed significant numbers of foreign visitors were unhappy with the quality and cost of their hotel rooms, especially in London.
